newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Boeing saga shows Van Miert is Europe's strong man.
newsitem.headline: Boeing saga shows Van Miert is Europe's strong man.

text.p: Karel Van Miert emerged reinforced in his role as Europe's antitrust policeman after he wrung key concessions from Boeing Co in return for EU approval for its $15 billion merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp.

Visibly proud of the decision reached on Wednesday, Van Miert left no doubt he would have proposed banning the deal, no matter the political pressure from the United States, if the U.S. aircraft giant had failed to offer the necessary commitments.

"On two of the points the solution found was satisfactory and on another point it was spectacular," he said. The last point was Boeing's last-ditch proposal to scrap exclusive supply pacts signed with three major U.S. airlines.
"If Boeing had not offered those remedies, I would have proposed today a negative decision despite all the pressure, all the phone calls," Van Miert told a news conference.
U.S. President Bill Clinton and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright telephoned several EU leaders, including Italy's Prime Minister Romano Prodi, on the Boeing merger.
Van Miert was speaking after the Commission, the EU's competition watchdog, gave its preliminary accord to the merger.

Besides the exclusive pacts, the agreement also implies Boeing will license patents obtained under U.S.-funded defence contracts and will keep McDonnell Douglas's civil aviation operations in a separate legal entity to avoid any leverage on airlines currently flying Douglas planes.
European Commission President Jacques Santer hailed Van Miert's role in securing a solution that preserves fair competition in Europe.
"The Commission has strongly thanked Mr Van Miert for his remarkable work and for the strong way in which he led negotiations," he said in a statement.
A Brussels-based aviation expert thought that Boeing had lost the game of chicken it has been playing with the EU in the last few months.
"If what I understand is correct, Boeing caved in," the expert said.

French Minister Pierre Moscovici struck a discording note, saying earlier on Wednesday he did not think Boeing's latest offer was sufficient. Some Brussels-based lawyers also said it was more a face-saving compromise than a real concession.
But shrugging off any criticism, Van Miert claimed no individual EU state would have obtained a similar result, an opinion apparently shared by Austrian Chancellor Viktor Klima.

"This is a very clear and positive message that Europe can use its joint strength to ensure major trading partners become involved in negotiations," Klima told a news conference after meeting Santer on separate issues.

Van Miert, a former Belgian socialist leader who has been in charge of European competition policy since 1993, has become increasingly more confident in performing the tasks of cracking open illegal cartels, clamping down on national subsidies to ailing industries and forcing strict conditions on mergers.

He has also consistently shown he is totally immune to political pressure, notably by chastising repeated French bailouts of Credit Lyonnais, once Europe's largest bank, or by accusing German carmaker Volkswagen -- the object of a bitter dispute last year over illegal subsidies -- of being a state within the state.
Referring to Tuesday's high-level phone calls from the United States, he said: "It is remarkable they have not called me.

Van Miert did not mince his words on Boeing, which made concessions only after realising the political pressure would not shake the Commission's determination. "Boeing is a private company but it seems to behave as if it was a public one," he said.
Nor did he spare the Federal Trade Commission of the United States which cleared the merger without conditions.
"It is surprising that a country which usually teaches the others lessons in the competition area was so reluctant in this case," he said.

Taking the lead as the world's most ardent defender of fair competition, Van Miert renewed an old call for a worldwide antitrust authority, possibly within the World Trade Organisation -- a call which has met with some U.S. scepticism.
"I was very astonished when on the American side they were talking about taking the issue to the WTO," Van Miert said.
Clinton warned this week he would examine all possible retaliatory measures if the the EU banned the merger including the Geneva trade body.
"We have been saying that maybe it would not be a bad idea to create a separate authority within the WTO to deal with competition, but they were not too keen on this," Van Miert said.
